j5.9: After all the blocks, the vector for “på” has picked up the context from the other words. The last row is now enough to guess the continuation.
j5.10: Right after the embedding the rows are independent of each other. “på” only knows that it is a preposition.
j5.14: One block gives a single round: each token can fetch information from other tokens and process it once, but never build further on what it fetched.
j5.15: A few rounds are enough for simple connections, such as linking “den” to “Katten”. Longer chains of inference do not fit.
j5.16: More rounds make room for chains: first find what “den” refers to, then what is known about it, then what usually follows.
j5.17: L = {{n}}. Every token passes through all the blocks in turn. The blocks cannot run in parallel for the same token, because each block needs the previous block’s result.
j5.18: The starting point: five integers, one per token. No vectors yet.
j5.19: Each id becomes a row of 4096 numbers. This is where the stream x is born.
j5.20: Block 1 has added two contributions. The content has changed, the shape has not.
j5.21: The same shape again. That is why the output of block 2 can go straight into block 3.
j5.22: The last block. The stream has received 64 contributions on top of the embedding.
j5.23: The stream is normalized a single time. Still the same shape.
j5.24: Here, and only here, the shape changes form: 4096 numbers per row become 128,256, one per token in the vocabulary.
j5.25: To generate, only the row for the last token is needed. It goes to sampling.
j5.30: Pre-norm: the stream can grow freely, but every block reads a normalized copy of size 1. That is why a final norm is needed before the LM head.
j5.31: Post-norm: the stream itself is normalized after every addition, so it is held at size 1 all the way. The direct path through the stream is disturbed in every block, which makes very deep models harder to train.
